text: The first partition of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1772 had dramatically reduced
one of Europe's largest states. But the Commonwealth had not disappeared. Despite
losing large areas of its territory, it continued to exist as an independent political
state. Its people, its institutions, and its rulers still hoped that the country could
recover its strength. Yet the powers surrounding it had other plans. Russia and Prussia continued
to view the weakened Commonwealth as a valuable opportunity for territorial expansion, and Austria,
which had participated in the first partition, remained deeply interested in the balance of
power in Central Europe. To understand how Poland-Lithuania eventually disappeared from
the map, we must look at the dramatic events of the 1790s. After the first partition,
the Commonwealth faced enormous political and economic challenges. Its government was weak,
its territory had been reduced, and foreign influence remained deeply embedded in its
political system. For years, reformers had argued that the country needed a stronger
central government, a more effective administration, and an army capable of defending its independence.
Their greatest opportunity came in 1791. On the 3rd of May, the Commonwealth adopted
a new constitution. It was one of the first modern written constitutions in Europe,
and aimed to reform the political system, strengthen the monarchy, and reduce the
destructive influence of foreign powers. For many supporters, it represented a chance to
rebuild the state. But the reforms threatened powerful interests, both inside and outside the
Commonwealth. Among their opponents were conservative nobles who feared losing their
traditional privileges. With support from Catherine II of Russia, these opponents formed the
Russian forces entered the Commonwealth, beginning a war against the supporters of the new
constitution. The Polish-Lithuanian army resisted, but the military situation became
increasingly difficult. King Stanisław August Poniatowski eventually joined the Targovica
Confederation, hoping to prevent further destruction. The constitution was effectively
overturned. The reform movement had been defeated. But Russia was not finished.
In 1793, Russia and Prussia carried out the second partition of the Polish-Lithuanian
Commonwealth. Unlike the first partition, Austria did not participate in this agreement.
This time, the two powers took enormous additional territories. Prussia seized the region
of Greater Poland, including the important cities of Gdańsk and Torun, as well as further
territories in the west. Russia acquired extensive areas in the east, including much
of present-day Belarus and parts of Ukraine. The Commonwealth was reduced to a fraction of
its former size. Its access to important economic regions was severely restricted,
and its political independence became increasingly dependent on Russian power.
The remaining state was now little more than a weakened territory under foreign supervision.
In 1793, representatives of the Commonwealth were forced to accept the territorial changes
at the Grodno Sejm. Russian pressure and military intimidation left little room for genuine
political independence. The second partition had effectively destroyed the remaining hopes of
restoring the country's sovereignty through ordinary political reform. But not everyone
was willing to accept this fate. In 1794, resistance turned into open rebellion.
The uprising was led by Tadeusz Kosciuszko, a military commander who had gained experience
fighting for independence during the American Revolutionary War. On the 24th of March,
he announced an uprising in Krakow. His goal was to defend the remaining Commonwealth,
resist foreign domination, and restore national independence. The rebellion quickly spread.
Soldiers, townspeople, and peasants joined the struggle. At the Battle of Racławice,
Polish forces achieved an important early victory against Russian troops. The uprising inspired
people across the country. For a moment, it seemed possible that the Commonwealth might survive.
But the military balance was overwhelmingly against the rebels. Russia and Prussia joined
forces against the uprising. Their armies advanced, while the rebellion struggled with
limited resources, internal divisions, and a lack of international support.
In October 1794, Kosciuszko was defeated and captured at the Battle of Maciejowice.
The uprising gradually collapsed. Warsaw was taken by Russian forces,
and the rebellion came to a brutal end. The final opportunity to save the Commonwealth
had disappeared. In 1795, Russia, Prussia, and Austria agreed to carry out the Third Partition.
This was the final division of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Russia acquired further territories in the east. Prussia took additional lands in the west,
including Warsaw. Austria received territories in the south, including areas around Krakow.
For the first time in centuries, the Polish-Lithuanian state ceased to exist as an
independent political entity. Its territory had been divided between three neighboring empires.
King Stanisław August Poniatowski abdicated on the 25th of November 1795. He was taken to
Russia, where he spent the final years of his life. The Commonwealth, which had once been one
the largest political powers in Europe, had disappeared from the map.
But the disappearance of the state did not mean the disappearance of its people.
Poles and Lithuanians continued to live under Russian, Prussian, and Austrian rule.
Their languages, traditions, and cultural identities survived, even as the new rulers attempted to
reorganize the territories they had acquired. Families found themselves living under different
administrations. Former political institutions were dismantled, and new laws and systems of
government were introduced. For many, the partitions meant the loss of political freedom.
For others, they brought uncertainty, resistance, and the difficult task of adapting to a new
reality. The memory of the Commonwealth, however, remained powerful. Throughout the 19th century,
uprisings and independence movements would challenge the rule of the partitioning powers.
The struggle for Polish independence continued for generations. Lithuanian national identity
also endured, and would later develop into its own movement for political independence.
The partitions of 1772, 1793, and 1795 transformed the political map of Europe.
Three neighboring powers had dismantled a state that had existed for centuries.
Yet they could not simply erase its history, its culture, or the identities of its people.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth had vanished from the map.
But the idea of its independence survived. And for more than a century,
that idea would remain alive in the hearts and minds of those who refused to forget it.
